method: A jump ring is a coil of wire cut into single turns, so the wire a ring consumes is the circumference measured through the middle of the wire, pi times the mandrel diameter plus one wire diameter, plus the kerf the saw removes from that turn. The ring count is the wire length in millimetres divided by that figure and rounded down to a whole ring, because a partial turn cannot be closed into a ring; the remainder is reported as leftover wire. The outer diameter is the mandrel plus two wire diameters, and the coil length is the ring count times the wire diameter, which is the coil's length while the turns still touch. The aspect ratio is the inner diameter divided by the wire diameter, the figure chainmail makers quote when comparing rings; this page reports it and does not judge which weaves a ring suits. Spring-back leaves a coiled ring slightly wider than its mandrel and hand coiling compresses the wire, so the result is a planning figure, not a measurement: cut a short test coil and measure it before a long run. The page does not model wire hardness, coil gaps, saw blade wander or metal loss from pickling, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
